background processes). A legitimate PyTorch model should only reference torch, numpy,
collections, and a small set of standard serialization helpers. Any import outside
this expected set is a strong indicator of malicious intent.
signatures.rule:
Model file (.bin, .pkl, .pickle, .pt, .pth) contains pickled objects with GLOBAL or
STACK_GLOBAL opcodes referencing modules outside the expected set for ML models.
Suspicious imports include: ctypes, importlib, zipimport, code, codeop, compileall,
webbrowser, antigravity, smtplib, ftplib, telnetlib, xmlrpc, multiprocessing,
_thread, signal, resource, gc (with set_debug), sys (with path manipulation)
Expected/safe modules: torch, numpy, collections, _codecs, copy_reg, sklearn

signatures.title: Pickle model opens network connections or makes HTTP requests on deserialization
signatures.description:
This rule detects model files that establish network connections when deserialized.
A malicious pickle payload can open raw sockets, make HTTP requests, or initiate
reverse shells — all triggered silently when a researcher runs torch.load(). Network
access during model loading enables command-and-control communication, credential
exfiltration to remote servers, downloading second-stage malware, and DNS-based data
exfiltration. Legitimate model files never need to make network connections during
deserialization — any network activity in a pickle stream is a definitive indicator
of malicious intent.
signatures.rule:
Model file (.bin, .pkl, .pickle, .pt, .pth) contains pickled objects referencing
any of: socket.socket, socket.create_connection, urllib.request.urlopen,
urllib.request.Request, http.client.HTTPConnection, http.client.HTTPSConnection,
requests.get, requests.post, requests.Session, httpx.Client, aiohttp.ClientSession
Detection via: pickletools.dis() output or binary scan for these module.function
pairs in the pickle opcode stream

signatures.title: HuggingFace model uses pickle serialization without safetensors alternative
signatures.description:
Python's pickle serialization format allows arbitrary code execution when deserialized.
A malicious actor can publish a model on HuggingFace with a .bin or .pkl file that
executes attacker code when loaded via torch.load() or any pickle.load() call.
The safetensors format (developed by HuggingFace) is the safe alternative — it is
pure tensor data with no code execution capability. Any model that ships .bin files
without a .safetensors alternative and without documented justification should be
treated as potentially malicious. This attack vector requires no vulnerability — it is
the intended behaviour of pickle.
signatures.rule:
Model repository contains any of: pytorch_model.bin, model.pkl, weights.pkl, *.pkl
AND does NOT contain a .safetensors equivalent
AND config.json has safe_serialization: false OR safe_serialization is absent
AND model card does not document the reason for non-safetensors format

signatures.title: Pickle model file contains os.system or subprocess calls for command execution
signatures.description:
This rule detects model files serialized with Python pickle that contain references to
os.system(), subprocess.Popen(), or related command execution functions. When a user
loads the model with torch.load() or pickle.load(), the pickled os.system call executes
arbitrary shell commands — installing backdoors, downloading second-stage payloads,
establishing reverse shells, or exfiltrating environment credentials. This is the most
direct form of pickle-based code execution and has been found in malicious models
uploaded to HuggingFace Hub targeting popular model name typosquats.
signatures.rule:
Model file (.bin, .pkl, .pickle, .pt, .pth) contains pickled objects referencing
any of: os.system, os.popen, subprocess.Popen, subprocess.call, subprocess.run,
subprocess.check_output, commands.getoutput, or pty.spawn
Detection via: pickletools.dis() output contains "os\nsystem", "subprocess\nPopen",
"subprocess\ncall", "subprocess\nrun", or binary grep for these module.function pairs
in the pickle opcode stream

signatures.title: Model advertised as SafeTensors but ships pickle files alongside for execution
signatures.description:
This rule detects a bait-and-switch attack where a model repository appears to use the
safe SafeTensors format but also includes pickle-serialized files that may be loaded
instead. The attacker publishes a model with both formats, but configures the model
card, config.json, or a custom loading script to prefer the pickle file — which contains
malicious code. Users see ".safetensors" in the file listing and assume the model is
safe, but the actual loading path deserializes the pickle. This bypass is especially
effective against automated scanners that check only for the presence of safetensors
files without verifying they are the files actually loaded.
signatures.rule:
Model repository contains .safetensors files AND also contains .bin, .pkl, .pickle,
.pt, or .pth files in the same directory or a subdirectory
AND the config.json or model loading code references the pickle-format file
(e.g., torch_dtype, weights_file, or custom loading script pointing to .bin)
OR the pickle file has a more recent modification timestamp than the safetensors file
OR the pickle file contains different weight checksums than the safetensors file

signatures.title: Tokenizer config contains malicious pre/post processing code or prompt injection
signatures.description:
This rule detects tokenizer configuration files with malicious pre-processing code,
injected chat templates, or poisoned special tokens. The tokenizer runs before every
LLM inference call, making it a persistent and invisible attack vector. A poisoned
chat_template in tokenizer_config.json can inject hidden system instructions into every
prompt. Malicious normalizer rules can silently transform user input. Custom pre/post
processors with embedded scripts execute arbitrary code during tokenization. Because
tokenizer files are JSON, they bypass pickle scanners entirely — yet they run code
and manipulate every input to the model.
signatures.rule:
Tokenizer files (tokenizer.json, tokenizer_config.json, special_tokens_map.json)
in a model repository contain any of:
- "pre_tokenizer" or "post_processor" with "type": "Script" or inline code blocks
- chat_template field containing injection patterns: hidden system messages,
  "ignore previous instructions", or template logic that appends invisible text
- added_tokens with content containing prompt injection or control sequences
- special_tokens_map entries with values containing URLs, shell commands, or
  base64-encoded strings
- tokenizer.json with a normalizer containing Unicode manipulation rules that
  transform safe-looking input into malicious sequences
